lessons.title: Communities and environmental factors
lessons.summary: A population is one species in an area; a community includes all populations; an ecosystem includes the non-living environment.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: A population is one species in an area; a community includes all populations; an ecosystem includes the non-living environment. Plants compete for light, water, minerals and space; animals for food, mates and territory. Interdependence links species through feeding, pollination and shelter.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Biotic factors include predators, pathogens and competitors. Abiotic factors include temperature, light, oxygen, water and pH. Changing one factor may affect many populations. Stability means relatively balanced populations, not numbers that never vary.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Levels of organisation. Individual → population → community → ecosystem. A habitat is the place where an organism lives.

Interdependence in action. In a woodland, trees provide food and shelter; insects pollinate flowers; birds disperse seeds; decomposers recycle nutrients. Removing one species, such as bees, can reduce plant reproduction and affect animals that eat fruits and seeds.

Abiotic and biotic factors to name. Abiotic: light intensity, temperature, moisture, soil pH and mineral content, wind intensity and direction, CO₂ for plants, O₂ for aquatic animals. Biotic: availability of food, new predators, new pathogens, one species outcompeting another.

lessons.title: Adaptations and extremophiles
lessons.summary: Adaptations can be structural, behavioural or functional.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Adaptations can be structural, behavioural or functional. Link a feature to its environmental challenge and survival benefit. Thick insulation conserves thermal energy; nocturnal activity can avoid daytime heat. Individuals do not acquire inherited adaptations simply because they need them.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Extremophiles inhabit conditions such as high heat, pressure or salinity. Desert plants may have waxy cuticles, reduced leaves and water stores. Trade-offs matter: reducing leaf area conserves water but can reduce light capture. Different adaptations may solve the same problem.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Three types of adaptation. Structural: features of body shape or structure, such as thick fur, small ears in the Arctic fox, or spines in cacti. Behavioural: actions such as migration, hibernation or burrowing. Functional: processes such as producing concentrated urine, or reproduction timed to food supply.

Surface area to volume and heat. Large animals with small ears and compact bodies have a small SA:V and lose less heat (polar bear). Desert animals like the fennec fox have large ears to radiate heat.

Extremophiles. Bacteria in hot vents, deep-sea organisms at high pressure, and organisms in very salty lakes have enzymes and membranes suited to these conditions.

lessons.title: Food chains and predator–prey cycles
lessons.summary: Producers make biomass, usually by photosynthesis.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Producers make biomass, usually by photosynthesis. Primary consumers eat producers and secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Arrows show biomass movement from food to feeder. Food webs represent several linked feeding relationships.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: More prey can support predator reproduction; more predators can reduce prey, after which predators may decline through food shortage. Changes lag rather than occurring instantly. Weather, disease and competition also influence real populations, so simple cycles are models.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Trophic language. Producer → primary consumer (herbivore) → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer. Apex predators are carnivores with no predators. Decomposers break down dead material.

Predator–prey graphs. The prey peak comes first; the predator peak follows because predators need time to breed. Predator numbers are usually lower than prey numbers.

Food web reasoning. When one population changes, follow every arrow into and out of it. A fall in rabbits might mean foxes eat more voles, so voles fall as well.

keypoints: Producers make biomass, usually by photosynthesis.
More prey can support predator reproduction; more predators can reduce prey, after which predators may decline through food shortage.

lessons.title: Quadrats, transects and abundance

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Use random coordinates to avoid choosing favourable quadrat locations. Count consistently and repeat widely. Mean count divided by quadrat area gives density; density times habitat area estimates population. Uneven distribution makes this an estimate, not an exact census.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: A transect investigates distribution along a gradient. Use quadrats at measured intervals and measure the relevant abiotic factor. Repeat transects and standardise counting rules. A correlation with light does not rule out variation in moisture or soil.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Required practical: random sampling. Lay two tape measures at right angles to make a grid. Use random number tables or a calculator to generate coordinates. Place a quadrat at each coordinate and count the species. Repeat for at least 10 quadrats.

Transects. Lay a tape from one habitat to another (for example shade to open field), place quadrats at regular intervals and record species and an abiotic factor (light meter, soil moisture). Abundance can be recorded as count or percentage cover.

lessons.title: Carbon and water cycles
lessons.summary: Photosynthesis incorporates atmospheric carbon into biomass; feeding passes it between organisms.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Photosynthesis incorporates atmospheric carbon into biomass; feeding passes it between organisms. Respiration by plants, animals and decomposers returns carbon dioxide. Decomposition returns mineral ions to soil; combustion releases stored carbon dioxide. Matter is recycled rather than created.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Evaporation and transpiration transfer water to air, condensation forms clouds and precipitation returns it. Runoff and soil movement return water to rivers and oceans. Materials cycle, whereas energy eventually dissipates to surroundings and is not recycled in the same way.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Carbon cycle processes. Photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration by plants, animals and microorganisms returns CO₂; feeding passes carbon compounds along food chains; death and decay pass carbon to decomposers; combustion of wood and fossil fuels releases CO₂. Fossil fuels formed from organisms that did not decay.

Water cycle. Evaporation from seas, transpiration from plants, condensation into clouds, precipitation, and runoff or percolation through soil. Water is used by plants for photosynthesis and support (turgor) and by animals for many processes.

Why decomposers matter. They return carbon to the atmosphere and mineral ions to the soil, which plants then absorb.

Evaporation and transpiration transfer water to air, condensation forms clouds and precipitation returns it.

lessons.title: Biodiversity, pollution and land use
lessons.summary: Biodiversity is the variety of species.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Biodiversity is the variety of species. It supports stable food webs and resources such as food and potential medicines. Human population growth and consumption increase waste, including sewage, fertilisers, toxic chemicals, smoke and acidic gases.

notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Farming, building, quarrying and waste disposal can destroy habitats. Deforestation reduces habitats and releases carbon through burning or decay. Peat stores partly decomposed carbon; draining or extracting it damages habitats and releases carbon dioxide. Explain both ecological effects and the demands driving land use.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Pollution types. Water: sewage, fertiliser runoff and toxic chemicals. Land: landfill and toxic chemicals. Air: smoke and acidic gases (sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides) causing acid rain.

Eutrophication. Fertiliser runoff → algae grow rapidly → algae block light → plants below die → decomposers feed on dead plants and use up oxygen → fish die.

Deforestation. Large-scale clearing in tropical areas for cattle, rice and biofuel crops reduces biodiversity, increases CO₂ (less photosynthesis, burning and decay) and removes carbon stores.

Peat. Peat bogs store carbon; draining them for agriculture or extracting peat for compost releases CO₂ and destroys habitats. Gardeners can choose peat-free compost.

lessons.title: Climate and maintaining biodiversity
lessons.summary: Increasing greenhouse gases contribute to higher global temperature.

notes.title: Understand the biology
notes.html: Increasing greenhouse gases contribute to higher global temperature. Changing climate can alter distribution, migration and food availability and increase extinction risk. notes.title: Apply and explain
notes.html: Breeding programmes, protected habitats, restoration, hedgerows and field margins can support biodiversity. Reducing deforestation, emissions and waste can reduce damage. Compare ecological benefits with cost, housing or food-production needs to make a reasoned judgement.

notes.title: Go deeper
notes.html:
Biological consequences of global warming. Loss of habitat when low-lying areas flood; changes in distribution as species move to cooler areas; changes in migration patterns; reduced biodiversity; spread of pests and diseases into new regions.

Programmes to protect biodiversity. Breeding programmes for endangered species; protection and regeneration of rare habitats; reintroduction of field margins and hedgerows where there is monoculture; reduction of deforestation and carbon emissions; recycling instead of landfill.

Conflicting pressures. Protecting biodiversity can conflict with needs for food, housing, jobs and income; conservation can cost money; monitoring is needed.

practical.title: Acceleration
method: Clamp a pulley to the end of the bench. Attach a string to the trolley, pass it over the pulley and tie it to a mass hanger.
Fix a card of known length (5.0 cm) on top of the trolley. Set up two light gates so the card passes through both, and connect them to a data logger.
Tilt the runway slightly so the trolley just keeps moving at a steady speed when pushed. This compensates for friction.
To vary the force: put five 20 g masses on the system. Move masses one at a time from the trolley to the hanger, so the total mass being accelerated stays the same.
Release the trolley from the same place each time. Record the time for the card to pass each gate and the time between the gates.
Calculate each speed (v = card length ÷ time at gate) and the acceleration a = (v₂ − v₁) ÷ t.
To vary the mass: keep the hanging mass the same and add masses to the trolley.
Plot acceleration against force, and acceleration against 1 ÷ mass.

practical.title: Waves
method: Ripple tank: set up the tank with about 1 cm of water, a lamp above it and a sheet of white paper underneath. Use a straight dipper connected to a signal generator.
Switch on and adjust the frequency until you can see clear wave shadows on the paper. Record the frequency from the signal generator.
Place a ruler on the paper. Measure across as many waves as possible (for example 10) and divide by the number of waves to find the wavelength. A photo of the pattern makes this easier.
Calculate the wave speed with v = f × λ. Repeat for different frequencies.
Waves on a string: attach a string to a vibration generator, pass it over a pulley and hang masses on the end to keep it taut.
Switch on the signal generator and adjust the frequency until a clear standing wave appears.
Measure the length of a whole number of half wavelengths (loops) with a metre rule. Wavelength = 2 × length ÷ number of loops.
Calculate the speed using v = f × λ.

Wavelength

method: Place the Leslie cube on a heat-proof mat. Fill it with very hot water from a kettle and put the lid on.
Point the infrared detector at one face of the cube, at a fixed distance (for example 10 cm). Record the reading.
Turn the cube so each face in turn points at the detector, keeping the distance the same. Record each reading.
Take the readings quickly so the water temperature stays almost the same.
Compare the readings to rank the surfaces from best to worst emitter of infrared radiation.
